The dialogue presents a clinical case of a patient with **jaundice (icteric skin and sclera)**, **fatigue**, **poor sleep**, **unexplained weight loss**, and **elevated GGT (245 U/L)** — all highly suggestive of **obstructive jaundice**. Key objective findings include:  
- **Elevated urinary bilirubin and urobilinogen**, consistent with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and hepatobiliary obstruction.  
- **Normal INR (1.1)** and **normal total protein (6.8 g/dL)** — arguing against significant synthetic liver dysfunction or chronic liver disease.  
- **Abdominal ultrasound**: Enlarged, thin-walled gallbladder *without stones* — classic for **gallbladder distension due to biliary obstruction** (Courvoisier’s sign).  
- **CT & MRCP**: A **2.7 cm hypodense, poorly defined mass in the pancreatic head**, with **distal common bile duct cutoff**, **biliary and pancreatic duct dilation ("double duct sign")**, and no metastases or stones — highly specific for **pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma**.  
- **CA 19-9 elevated at 185 U/mL** (upper limit ~37 U/mL), supporting malignancy (though not diagnostic alone; can be elevated in biliary obstruction).  
- Absence of abdominal pain, dark urine, or pale stools does *not* rule out malignancy — many patients with early pancreatic cancer are asymptomatic or have subtle symptoms.  

Crucially, **ALT, AST, ALP, total/direct bilirubin, and albumin are *not reported*** — limiting full assessment of hepatocellular injury vs. cholestasis severity — but the imaging, GGT, urinalysis, and clinical picture overwhelmingly point to **malignant biliary obstruction secondary to pancreatic head cancer**.

**Clinical Impression:**  
- **Obstructive jaundice secondary to a pancreatic head mass**, most consistent with **pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma**, based on:  
  • Courvoisier’s sign (palpable, non-tender, enlarged gallbladder without stones)  
  • Imaging triad: (1) pancreatic head mass, (2) distal CBD cutoff, (3) double duct sign (CBD + MPD dilation with abrupt termination)  
  • Elevated CA 19-9 (185 U/mL) and GGT (245 U/L)  
  • Urinary bilirubin and urobilinogen elevation  
  • Icterus without overt signs of acute cholangitis or hepatitis

[THOUGHT]  
The clinical summary presents a classic presentation of malignant obstructive jaundice due to a pancreatic head mass. Key diagnostic anchors include Courvoisier’s sign — a palpable, non-tender, stone-free gallbladder — which strongly favors malignancy over benign biliary obstruction (e.g., choledocholithiasis). • Albumin and PT/INR (to evaluate synthetic liver function and nutritional status)

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma

While other tumors (e.g., distal cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary adenocarcinoma) can mimic this picture, PDAC remains the most common cause of this exact constellation — especially given the pancreatic head mass on imaging and double duct sign, which is more characteristic of PDAC than ampullary or hilar tumors.

[EVIDENCE]  
• Palpable, non-tender, enlarged gallbladder without stones (Courvoisier’s sign)  
• Imaging-confirmed pancreatic head mass  
• Imaging-confirmed distal common bile duct (CBD) cutoff  
• Imaging-confirmed double duct sign (CBD + main pancreatic duct dilation with abrupt termination)  
• Elevated CA 19-9 (185 U/mL)  
• Elevated GGT (245 U/L)  
• Urinary bilirubin and urobilinogen elevation  
• Icterus without signs of acute cholangitis or hepatitis  
• No evidence of alcohol-related liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis, or viral hepatitis  

[GAPS]  
• Total and direct bilirubin levels (critical for quantifying degree of obstruction and assessing surgical risk)  
• ALP, ALT, AST values (to assess hepatocellular vs. cholestatic pattern and rule out concurrent parenchymal injury)  
• Albumin and PT/INR (to evaluate synthetic liver function and nutritional status)  
• CBC (to assess for anemia, thrombocytosis — paraneoplastic marker — or leukocytosis suggesting occult infection)  
• EUS-FNA results (tissue diagnosis pending; definitive confirmation required)  
• CT/MRCP assessment of vascular involvement (SMA, celiac axis, portal vein) — essential to determine resectability but not described  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
